ancient.name: Seh Gabi 21
ancient.story_individual: Seh Gabi 21 are fetal remains estimated to be 35 weeks old, he was possibly stillborn or died during childbirth. Seh Gabi 21 was discovered among a series of mounds near the Gamas Ab river in Western Iran. His remains are approximately 6,000 years old during an era known as the Chalcolithic in Iran.

ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

famous.name: Galgedil man
famous.story_individual:
The Galgedil man lived between 900 and 1000 CE during the Viking Age and was found in the region now known as Galgedil, Funen, Denmark.

Remarkably, the study “Population genomics of the Viking world” by Margaryan et al. 2020, in which Viking age remains from around Europe were DNA tested, found that the man from Galgedil in Denmark (Galgedil AXE or VK279) was closely related to another man, Oxford 8 (VK144), found in the Viking age mass burial in St John’s College, Oxford, England. The mass burial contained over 30 young men with Scandinavian ancestry. One theory is that they were killed during the St. Brice's Day massacre on 13 November 1002 when the King of England, Æthelred the Unready, ordered the mass killing of all Danes.

Genetic analysis showed that the two men were second-degree relatives, meaning that they were either half brothers, uncle and nephew, or grandparent and grandson. Their Y-DNA haplogroups are nearly identical with the only difference being the haplogroup resolution due to different Y-chromosome coverage, while their mtDNA haplogroups are entirely different. This suggests that they had a patrilineal relationship, such as half-brothers with the same father and different mothers.

Sculptor and archaeologist Oscar D. Nilsson reconstructed the face of the Galgedil man (seen here), and the model is on display at the National Museum in Copenhagen. He was a heavy-set man with a number of marks from violence or battle. The Oxford man’s skull was incomplete and unfortunately could not be reconstructed.

The Oxford skeleton was brought to Copenhagen, and 1,000 years later, the two close relatives were reunited next to each other at the National Museum.

Galgedil AXE’s maternal line belonged to mtDNA haplogroup I4a*.

Reconstruction photo provided by O D Nilsson.

famous.name: Queen Noor of Jordan
famous.story_individual:
Queen Noor of Jordan (born Lisa Najeeb Halaby) is an American-born queen consort who became the fourth wife of King Hussein of Jordan in 1978. Before becoming queen, she graduated from Princeton University with a degree in Architecture and Urban Planning and worked in international urban planning.

Upon her marriage to King Hussein, she converted to Islam and took the name Noor Al-Hussein, which means "Light of Hussein." As Queen of Jordan, she focused on numerous social and cultural initiatives, including women's empowerment, education, public health, and environmental conservation. She established the Noor Al Hussein Foundation to support sustainable development and has been particularly active in promoting cross-cultural understanding between the Arab world and the West.

King Hussein's death in 1999 marked a transition in her role, as her stepson Abdullah II became king. Since then, Queen Noor has maintained an active international presence as a global humanitarian activist and advocate for peace. She serves on numerous international boards and is a prominent voice for nuclear disarmament, refugees' rights, and conflict prevention.

Queen Noor is the first Arab-American to become queen of an Arab country. Her father, Najeeb Halaby, was a prominent Syrian-American aviation pioneer who served as head of the Federal Aviation Administration under President Kennedy.

Today, Queen Noor divides her time between Jordan, the United States, and the United Kingdom, continuing her work in global humanitarian causes and cross-cultural dialogue.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was revealed on the Faces of America TV show.

famous.name: Ernest Wejher
famous.story_individual:
Ernest Wejher, sometimes spelled Weyher, was a Polish nobleman, military commander, and statesman from the Pomeranian branch of the Wejher family. He held the position Starost of Puck from 1582 to 1598.

He served as a courtier and advisor to King Sigismund II August in his youth and later played a significant military role under King Stephen Báthory. He participated in several campaigns, including the Livonian War (1558-1583) against Russia, the 1576-1577 expedition against Gdańsk, and the 1577 campaign toward Moscow, where he commanded about 1,000 German landsknechts.

Ernest Wejher was a patron of the arts and supported the Catholic Church after his 1585 conversion, funding the construction of a chapel in Puck in 1599 and engaging in charitable works. The Wejher family, with spellings like Weyher and Weiher, rose to prominence in Pomerania during the 13th and 14th centuries, maintaining influence in Polish politics through the 16th and 17th centuries with figures like Jakub and Ludwik Wejher, until their decline in the 18th century due to Poland's partitions.

A 2023 study by Blusiewicz et al. on the Weyher family crypt in Puck identified a male burial likely belonging to Ernest Wejher, with DNA testing revealing Y-DNA (G-FGC962/Z2022) and mtDNA (N1a1a1a1) haplogroups.

Reference

  • Blusiewicz, K., & et al. (2023). Interpretation of the burials from the crypt of the Weyher family in the Saint Apostles Peter and Paul Church in Puck. https://www.archeologia.uw.edu.pl/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Krypta-grobowa-rodu-Wejherow-1.pdf

famous.name: Zlatý kůň woman
famous.story_individual:
The Zlatý kůň woman lived approximately 45,000 years ago during the Upper Paleolithic period in what is now the Czech Republic. She belongs to one of the earliest groups of modern humans to venture into Europe after leaving Africa, carrying about 3% Neanderthal DNA from relatively recent interbreeding in her family line.

Her remains were discovered in 1950 in the Zlatý kůň cave (meaning "Golden Horse" in Czech). Initially, archaeologists found her skull split in half and believed the remains belonged to two different individuals. Only decades later, through genome sequencing, did they confirm it was a single person. After her death, her remains were gnawed by either a wolf or hyena, which damaged portions of her skull, particularly the left side of her face.

She lived during one of the coldest periods of the last ice age, surviving in harsh tundra conditions as part of a small hunter-gatherer group. She died as a young adult, though the cause of death remains unknown.

Facial reconstruction by Cicero Moraes, CC BY 4.0.

In 2023, researchers led by Cícero Moraes created a facial reconstruction using CT scans of her skull. The reconstruction revealed distinctive features that blur the line between modern humans and Neanderthals: she had a notably robust facial structure with a strong jawline that initially led experts to mistake her remains for those of a male. Her brain cavity was larger than that of modern humans in the comparative database, another trait showing Neanderthal affinity. While the exact colors of her features cannot be determined from available evidence, researchers created both a scientific grayscale model and a speculative version showing her with dark curly hair and brown eyes.

Her genome remains one of the oldest modern human genome ever sequenced, though her lineage appears not to have contributed significantly to later European populations. She represents a fascinating glimpse into the early history of modern humans in Europe and their interaction with Neanderthals.

famous.name: Aboriginal Lock
famous.story_individual:
In the early 1920s, a lock of hair was donated by an anonymous Aboriginal man from Golden Ridge, near Kalgoorlie in Western Australia, to British anthropologist Alfred Cort Haddon during a brief train stop. Preserved for nearly a century, this unassuming relic became a scientific treasure when, in 2011, researchers led by Eske Willerslev at the University of Copenhagen sequenced its DNA, unlocking the first complete Aboriginal Australian genome. Published in Science, the study revealed that Aboriginal Australians descended from an early human dispersal into Asia 62,000 to 75,000 years ago, distinct from the later wave that shaped modern Asian populations. With approval from the Goldfields Land and Sea Council, this hair lock—now a symbol of ancient lineage—highlighted one of the oldest continuous populations outside Africa, forever linking a simple gift to a profound chapter in human history.

famous.name: Ann Curry
famous.story_individual:
Ann Curry, born in Guam, is a distinguished American journalist known for her fearless reporting over a 45-year career covering human suffering in war zones and natural disasters. She has reported from numerous conflict areas including Kosovo, Iraq, Syria, Afghanistan, and Darfur, gaining recognition for her coverage of devastating events like the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and the 2010 Haiti earthquake. During her notable 25-year tenure at NBC News, she served as co-anchor of the Today show and anchor of Dateline NBC. After leaving NBC in 2015, she founded her own media startup and hosted shows including PBS's "We'll Meet Again" and TNT's "Chasing the Cure." Her accomplishments have earned her multiple Emmy Awards and the Murrow Lifetime Achievement Award.

Born to Hiroe Nagase, who is Japanese, and an American father, Curry's early life reflected her multicultural heritage. She spent her childhood between Japan, where she attended school on a U.S. naval base in Nagasaki, and various American cities. The family eventually settled in Oregon, where Curry completed high school before pursuing journalism at the University of Oregon. Her mtDNA haplogroup assignment N9a was shared during a 2005 interview with Dr. Spencer Wells of National Geographic's Genographic Project.

Pictured: Ann Curry (2022), Collision Conf, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Angela Buchdahl
famous.story_individual:
Rabbi Angela Buchdahl is the first Asian American to be ordained as a rabbi and the first to be ordained as a hazzan.

Born to a Korean mother and American father, Buchdahl was raised Jewish. Growing up, she struggled with her identity due to rejection from her peers as a non-Christian Korean immigrant to the US and from the Orthodox Jewish community, as she inherited her Jewish religion and Ashkenazi DNA from her father, not her mother. 

As a young woman, Buchdahl underwent a giryur to reaffirm her Jewish faith and pursued cantorial and rabbinic studies after graduating with a degree in Religious Studies from Yale University. 

In 2014, Buchdahl became the Senior Rabbi of the Central Synagogue in the Manhattan borough of New York City. The synagogue thrived under Buchdahl’s leadership, with attendance and retention doubling and tripling. 

A prominent voice in the Reform Jewish community, she was invited to lead the prayers of the White House Hannukkah celebration in 2014 and has been named one of America’s most influential rabbis. 

Angela Buchdahl’s mtDNA haplogroup was revealed in Finding Your Roots The Official Companion to the PBS Series by Henry Louis Gates, Jr.

Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia. Pictured: Cantor Angela Warnick Buchdahl, Jewish Women's Archive, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.
